title: Enzymes and metabolism
introduction: Learn how a folded active site accelerates chemistry, then reason with rate curves, experimental quantities and inhibition pathways.
prerequisites: Know how to calculate a graph gradient
objectives: Explain reaction-rate changes using catalytic mechanism
Interpret and calculate graph-based enzyme rates with units
HL: compare metabolic pathways, regulatory inhibition and antibiotic targets

sections.guidingQuestion: Why can living reactions proceed quickly without a catalyst changing the net energy balance?
sections.explanation:
A catalyst offers a reaction pathway with a lower activation-energy barrier and is regenerated after a catalytic cycle. Most biological enzymes are globular proteins. Reactions that proceed slowly without enzymes can then occur fast enough to support cellular survival, growth and repair.

Catalysis changes reaction rates, not the location of equilibrium or the net Gibbs-energy difference between starting materials and products. An enzyme is not a net fuel or source of the products' energy. A reaction can be thermodynamically unfavourable even when an enzyme is available; coupling to other reactions may be needed.

sections.workedExample: Digestive amylase accelerates starch breakdown but does not change the reaction's equilibrium constant.

misconceptions.correction: It reduces a kinetic barrier, not the product–reactant free-energy difference.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why does one organism require many different enzymes?
sections.explanation:
Metabolism is the interdependent network of chemical reactions in living systems. The product of one catalysed reaction may become the substrate for another, allowing branching pathways and linked biochemical cycles. Metabolism includes both energy transfer and the synthesis of cellular matter.

Active-site chemistry makes enzymes selective for reactions and substrates, so many distinct enzymes are necessary. Cells adjust enzyme abundance or activity to regulate throughput, substrate use and inter-pathway coordination. A metabolic network is not a single enzyme acting on all compounds.

sections.guidingQuestion: What distinguishes building from breaking down in metabolism?
sections.explanation:
Anabolism forms larger or more complex compounds from smaller precursors. Examples required by the guide include protein synthesis, glycogen formation and photosynthesis. Overall condensation schemes illustrate the formation of many macromolecules. Catabolism includes hydrolytic digestion of polymers and oxidative respiration of fuels.

Anabolic reactions commonly require input or coupling of energy; catabolic reactions can release usable energy. But not every biosynthetic step releases water in its direct mechanism, and not every catabolic reaction is hydrolysis. The labels describe the overall transformation and are not absolute claims about each individual bond change.

sections.guidingQuestion: How do amino acids far apart in sequence contribute to one active site?
sections.explanation:
An enzyme's active site is usually formed by a few appropriately placed amino-acid residues within a globular protein. Those residues can lie far apart along the primary sequence but meet when the polypeptide folds. The substrate binds where side-chain shape, charge and chemical groups permit selective catalysis.

The remaining residues maintain the active-site geometry through overall tertiary or quaternary interactions. Hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and hydrophobic packing help establish this fold. Denaturation or a distant mutation can therefore reduce enzyme activity even if residues that directly contact the substrate are unchanged.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is induced fit not a rigid lock-and-key animation?
sections.explanation:
Substrate binding can change the conformation of the enzyme and the bound substrate. Productive contacts strengthen, catalytic groups align and substrate bonds may be strained or polarised. The transient enzyme–substrate complex is formed as a consequence of both molecular recognition and flexibility.

Induced fit does not mean that the enzyme loses its fold or that every enzyme follows exactly the same sequential movements. It is an instructional model of conformational adjustment; depicting the active site as permanently rigid misstates the requirement that both enzyme and substrate can change shape.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can an immobilised enzyme still encounter its substrate?
sections.explanation:
Enzyme catalysis usually requires substrate molecules to encounter an available active site with suitable orientation and energy. Diffusion, mixing and molecular motion make encounters possible. More encounters can increase rate, but only some result in productive binding and catalysis.

Enzymes may be immobilised on membranes or artificial support beads, while large substrates may also be held in position. Relative movement and access matter: a substrate can diffuse to an enzyme that remains anchored. Immobilisation should not be confused with denaturation or chemical inactivation.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why can pH or heat destroy selective enzyme activity?
sections.explanation:
Substrate specificity depends on shape complementarity and active-site chemical groups, including charges, hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. Related substrates may sometimes be processed, so specificity need not mean an enzyme binds exactly one chemical species in all contexts.

Extreme temperature or pH can disturb intramolecular interactions, altering the active-site arrangement or ionisation and reducing catalytic activity. Low temperature by itself often decreases molecular movement without denaturing a protein. Denaturation may or may not be reversible, depending on the enzyme and conditions.

sections.guidingQuestion: How do we distinguish explanatory enzyme-rate models from experimental observations?
sections.explanation:
At modest temperatures, greater molecular motion often increases productive collision frequency. Strong heating can reduce active enzyme through unfolding; the position of an optimum depends on assay time and enzyme identity. Changes in pH affect ionisation and sometimes folding, producing an enzyme-specific pH optimum.

At a constant amount of active enzyme, rising substrate concentration usually increases initial reaction rate and approaches saturation. The three graphs are explicitly invented numerical models, not actual laboratory results. Their accompanying tables list every coordinate, labelled units and fixed assay assumptions so students can test the claimed relationships and compare them with future experimental data.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is the difference between an initial tangent and a full-experiment average?
sections.explanation:
A rate is a change in amount or concentration per unit time. A product amount–time curve has positive gradient; a substrate concentration–time curve falls and its negative gradient gives substrate disappearance rate. Always show units such as μmol min⁻¹ or mmol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

An initial rate corresponds to the tangent slope near the beginning of a reaction or a justified short near-linear interval. Later rates can fall as substrate is depleted or conditions change. A multi-minute secant gives the mean rate over that interval, not necessarily initial rate. The numerical curve below is a disclosed theoretical model, not measured observations.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why does the catalysed energy barrier fall while reaction ΔE stays constant?
sections.explanation:
Breaking or distorting bonds and reorganising charges on the way to a transition state requires an energy input, while forming more stable bonds can release energy. Enzymes favour a lower-barrier mechanistic route. Catalytic interactions can stabilise the transition state and speed conversion without being a net energy source.

The final reactant-to-product energy difference is unaffected by an enzyme. Our illustrative relative-energy profiles have reactants at 20, products at 0, an uncatalysed peak at 90 and a catalysed peak at 55 kJ mol⁻¹: barriers are 70 and 35, while both net energy differences are −20 kJ mol⁻¹. These are theoretical example values, not measured biochemical energetics.

Activation energy: barrier from reactants to transition state
sections.workedExample: From a common reactant baseline at 20, lowering a peak from 90 to 55 lowers activation energy 70→35 kJ mol⁻¹.

sections.guidingQuestion: What distinguishes cytosolic respiration from secreted gut digestion?
sections.explanation:
Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, and in eukaryotes the Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix. These are intracellular processes. Digestive enzymes act extracellularly within the gut lumen after being secreted from cells; enzyme synthesis and enzyme action can therefore happen in different compartments.

Secretory enzyme vesicles release their contents by exocytosis when they fuse with the plasma membrane. Hodder printed p. 396 incorrectly says endocytosis in this context; independent NCBI digestive-enzyme evidence specifies exocytosis. Endocytosis instead imports material into cells.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why does metabolism contribute to body temperature?
sections.explanation:
Metabolism transfers chemical energy to ATP, chemical gradients, mechanical work and other cellular functions. No biological energy-transfer process captures all available energy as organised work; some energy becomes dispersed as heat. This thermal output is a normal feature of metabolism, not energy creation by enzymes.

Birds, mammals and some other animals depend on ongoing metabolic heat production to support relatively constant body temperature. Heat output changes with activity and physiology. Individual pathways can have different energy budgets; do not assert that every metabolic reaction releases the same heat.

sections.guidingQuestion: What distinguishes a regenerated cycle from a reaction sequence with endpoints?
sections.explanation:
Glycolysis is a linear metabolic sequence that converts glucose toward pyruvate through enzyme-catalysed intermediate reactions. Cyclic pathways regenerate a participant needed for subsequent turns; the Krebs cycle regenerates oxaloacetate, and the Calvin cycle regenerates ribulose bisphosphate.

A metabolic cycle still has net inputs, outputs and energy requirements or releases. Its intermediates are not a perpetual supply of material. The guide uses these three pathways to illustrate linear versus cyclic organisation, not as a demand to memorise every intermediate in this topic.

sections.guidingQuestion: How does binding away from a catalytic pocket change enzyme activity?
sections.explanation:
An allosteric inhibitor binds at a specific noncatalytic site. The binding changes internal protein interactions and can alter the active-site conformation enough to reduce catalysis. In the guide's model this binding is reversible, so the inhibitor may dissociate and enzyme activity can recover.

A simple non-competitive diagram contrasts a separate regulatory site with direct active-site competition. Real allosteric regulation has multiple kinetic patterns, including mixed inhibition; the special pure noncompetitive model is not identical to every allosteric mechanism. An inhibitor must have binding specificity; arbitrary molecules cannot universally bind regulatory sites.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why can high substrate offset a reversible competitive inhibitor?
sections.explanation:
A competitive inhibitor reversibly occupies a substrate-binding region of the active site, blocking substrate access while present. Raising substrate concentration increases the chance of substrate rather than inhibitor binding. Under a simple Michaelis–Menten competitive model, Vmax remains the same while apparent Km rises.

Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, reducing endogenous cholesterol biosynthesis. The contrast with school-level non-competitive inhibition concerns where the inhibitor binds and how higher substrate concentration affects inhibition; real allosteric mechanisms cannot all be assigned one universal kinetic shape.

sections.guidingQuestion: How does a pathway product limit its own excessive production?
sections.explanation:
In isoleucine biosynthesis in bacteria, threonine undergoes a sequence of conversions catalysed by enzymes. Isoleucine, the end product, can bind allosterically to the first controlling enzyme, threonine deaminase, and decrease its activity when isoleucine accumulates.

This reversible negative feedback saves resources and reduces pathway flux before additional intermediates build up. When isoleucine levels decline, inhibitory occupancy can decrease and biosynthetic activity resumes. Feedback regulates an upstream step, not only the final chemical conversion.

sections.guidingQuestion: How does penicillin permanently impair bacterial cell-wall crosslinking?
sections.explanation:
Penicillin-class β-lactams inhibit susceptible penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan crosslinking. A catalytic active-site serine can react with the β-lactam to produce a covalently acylated, long-lived inactive enzyme complex. This is a mechanism-based, effectively irreversible inhibition rather than ordinary short-lived competition.

Some bacteria develop altered penicillin-binding proteins that bind/react with the antibiotic less effectively. Other bacteria produce β-lactamases that chemically break down β-lactam antibiotics. Altering the drug's target and destroying the drug are distinct resistance mechanisms; do not conflate either with a general change in the bacterial DNA replication mechanism.

summary: Catalysis lowers an activation barrier without changing equilibrium. Folded active sites and productive encounters control enzyme activity. Qualitative curves, controlled rate measurements and regulation illustrate metabolic interdependence.

notes: Mapped C1.1.1–C1.1.17 to official IB 2025 Guide with SL/HL boundaries.
Consulted full Hodder C1.1 pp. 380–404 (PDF 392–416); corrected exocytosis/endocytosis error on printed p. 396.
All graph curves are independently generated hypothetical model values with explicit units, assumptions and accessible numeric tables; none presented as laboratory measurements.
Qualified biochemistry, chemistry graph, IB assessment, rights and accessibility sign-off are still required.
No claims of laboratory validation, student testing or reviewer approval.
